title: Weighing coins
objectives: Find a fake coin in the fewest weighings by splitting into three groups.

screens.title: Nine coins, one heavy
screens.prose: Nine coins look alike, but one is heavier. A balance compares two groups and has three outcomes: left sinks, right sinks, or level. Each weighing below gives you its worst outcome.

state.caption: Nine coins, one heavier. Every coin is a suspect.

screens.question: Find the fake in two weighings.

ops.label: Weigh 4 against 4
ops.why: If the scale tips, 4 suspects remain for one weighing, and one weighing splits at most 3.

ops.label: Weigh 1 against 1
ops.why: If it balances, 7 suspects remain for one weighing, and one weighing splits at most 3.

canvas.caption: The left pan sank: coins 1, 2 and 3 are the suspects.

ops.label: Weigh all 3 again
ops.why: All three on the scale tells you nothing new. Put one against one and keep one aside.

canvas.caption: The left pan sank: coins 1 to 4 are the suspects.
Coins 1 and 2 are left, and no weighing remains.
It balanced: coins 3 and 4 are left, and no weighing remains.
It balanced: coins 3 to 9 are the suspects.
The left pan sank: coins 3, 4 and 5 are left.
It balanced: coins 7, 8 and 9 are left.
It balanced: coins 5 to 9 are left.
Coin 1 against coin 3 balanced, so coin 2 is the heavy fake.

hints.text: After the first weighing, how many suspects can one weighing still handle?
One weighing has three outcomes, so it can finish 3 suspects at most.
Weigh 3 against 3 first. Every outcome leaves 3 suspects; then weigh 1 against 1.

feedback.correct: Three against three, then one against one.
feedback.generic: Not there yet. The first weighing must leave at most 3 suspects whatever happens.

explain.text: Three against three leaves 3 suspects whatever happens: the heavier pan, or the 3 aside. One against one then finds the fake among 3. Principle: split into three groups as equal as possible.

screens.title: Twenty-seven coins
screens.prose: Now 27 coins, one heavier. Weigh 9 against 9 with 9 aside, as the tree shows.
screens.question: What is the fewest weighings that always finds the fake?

hints.text: Each outcome of the first weighing leaves 9 suspects.
Nine suspects took 2 weighings.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the first weighing, then what 9 suspects need.

byKey.five: That halves each time. Thirds are faster: 27, 9, 3, 1.
byKey.nine: Nine is how many suspects remain, not weighings.
byKey.two: Two weighings have $3^2 = 9$ outcomes, fewer than 27 suspects.

explain.text: Each outcome of 9 against 9 leaves 9 suspects, and 9 take 2 more weighings. So 27, 9, 3, 1 takes 3. Principle: each weighing cuts the suspects to a third.

screens.title: Twelve coins, heavy or light
screens.prose: Twelve coins, and one fake that may be heavier or lighter. You must find it and say which. That is 24 cases. First weigh coins 1 to 4 against 5 to 8: the left pan sinks.

state.caption: Coins 1 to 4 against 5 to 8. The left pan sank.

screens.question: How many cases remain?

widget.label: Cases
widget.accept: 8: 1 to 4 possibly heavy, 5 to 8 possibly light

hints.text: Which coins are cleared, and which could still be the fake?
Coins 9 to 12 sat aside, and the scale did not balance.
Each of 1 to 4 could be heavy; each of 5 to 8 could be light.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. List what each coin on the scale could still be.

byKey.four: You kept only the sinking side. A light coin on the right also sinks the left.
byKey.twelve: Coins 9 to 12 are cleared: the scale would have balanced without them.
byKey.sixteen: Each coin on the scale has one direction left, not two.

explain.text: The left sank. So the fake is 1 to 4 heavy or 5 to 8 light, and 9 to 12 are genuine. That is 8 cases, and two weighings give 9 outcomes, so the count still allows it.

screens.title: The second weighing
screens.prose: Eight cases remain: 1, 2, 3 or 4 heavy, or 5, 6, 7 or 8 light. Coin 9 is genuine. Weigh coins 1, 2 and 5 against 3, 6 and 9.
screens.question: How many cases does each outcome leave?

hints.text: Test each case: which pan would it make sink?
1 heavy sinks the left. 6 light also sinks the left.
Left: 1H, 2H, 6L. Right: 3H, 5L. Level: 4H, 7L, 8L.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put each of the 8 cases on the scale in your head.

byKey.r1c1: Right sinks if 3 is heavy or 5 is light: two cases.
byKey.r2c1: Level leaves the coins off the scale: 4 heavy, 7 light or 8 light.

explain.text: Left sinks: 1 or 2 heavy, or 6 light. Right sinks: 3 heavy or 5 light; level: 4 heavy, or 7 or 8 light. Each outcome keeps at most 3 cases, so one weighing finishes.

screens.title: Halve each time
screens.prose: Back to nine coins with one heavy fake. A candidate halves: 4 against 4, then 2 against 2, then 1 against 1. They announce 3 weighings.

state.caption: The halving plan: 4 against 4, coin 9 aside.

screens.question: What is the fewest weighings for nine coins?

options.why: You trusted halving. A balance has three outcomes, so thirds use the level outcome too.
You treated each weighing as a yes or no. A balance has three outcomes, so use $\log_3$.

hints.text: How many outcomes does one weighing have?
Three: left, right or level. Halving never uses level.
Thirds: 9, 3, 1. Two weighings, $3^2 = 9$ outcomes.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use all three outcomes of a weighing.

byKey.three: Halving wastes the level outcome. Three against three finishes in 2.
byKey.four: A balance is not a yes or no test. It has three outcomes, so $\log_3 9 = 2$.

explain.text: Halving uses only two outcomes of each weighing. Thirds use all three: 9, 3, 1 in 2 weighings, matching $3^2 = 9$. Principle: a test with three outcomes should split into thirds.

screens.title: Two coins, no help
screens.prose: Two coins, one fake that may be heavier or lighter, and no coin known to be genuine. You must name the fake.

state.caption: Coin 1 against coin 2: the left sinks.

screens.question: How many weighings does it take?

options.text: No number of weighings is enough

options.why: The scale tips, but a heavy left coin and a light right coin tip it the same way.
A second weighing of the same two coins repeats the same tilt.
More weighings of the same two coins add nothing.

hints.text: What can the scale do with only these two coins?
It can only weigh one against the other.
Left sinks fits coin 1 heavy and coin 2 light alike.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether any weighing separates 1 heavy from 2 light.

byKey.one: Left sinks fits both coin 1 heavy and coin 2 light.
byKey.two: Weighing again gives the same tilt.
byKey.three: Repeating the same weighing adds nothing.

explain.text: The only weighing is coin against coin, and 1 heavy and 2 light give the same tilt. No weighing ever separates those cases. Principle: count outcomes that differ, not weighings made.

screens.title: Three outcomes a weighing
screens.prose: A weighing has three outcomes, so $k$ weighings tell apart at most $3^k$ cases. $$\text{cases} \le 3^k$$ Split the suspects into three groups as equal as possible, so each outcome keeps at most a third. With one heavy fake, $n$ coins are $n$ cases.
screens.question: What is the fewest weighings for 81 coins with one heavy fake?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the smallest $k$ with $3^k \ge 81$.

byKey.three: Three weighings give 27 outcomes, fewer than 81 cases.

explain.text: Three weighings give $3^3 = 27$ outcomes, too few for 81 cases. Four give $3^4 = 81$, and thirds reach it: 81, 27, 9, 3, 1. The count is a bound and the thirds plan meets it.

screens.title: Why 13 coins fail
screens.prose: Thirteen coins, one fake heavier or lighter, three weighings, no extra genuine coin. That is 26 cases against 27 outcomes, yet it cannot be done. Order the proof; two lines may swap and one does not belong.
screens.question: Order the proof that 13 coins need more than 3 weighings.

lines.text: Say the first weighing puts $a$ coins on each pan.
A tilt leaves $2a$ cases for 2 weighings, so $2a \le 9$ and $a \le 4$.
Level leaves $13 - 2a$ coins with 2 cases each, so $26 - 4a \le 9$ and $a \ge 5$.
No whole number $a$ is at most 4 and at least 5.
So no first weighing works, and 13 coins need a fourth.
26 cases are more than 27 outcomes, so it fails at once.
lines.why: 26 is less than 27, so the count alone allows 13 coins. The first weighing is where it breaks.

hints.text: Name the first weighing, then bound each outcome.
Two weighings leave 9 outcomes for each branch.
Name $a$, bound it from the tilt and from level, then find the clash.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Bound $a$ from both outcomes before you conclude.

byKey.d1: 26 is fewer than 27. The count allows 13; the proof needs the first weighing.
byKey.left-out: Every line except the one comparing 26 with 27 belongs.

explain.text: Every branch must fit into $3^2 = 9$ outcomes. The tilt branch needs $a \le 4$ and the level branch $a \ge 5$, so no first weighing works. Principle: apply the count branch by branch, not only at the start.

screens.title: Drill: five weighings
screens.prose: Drill, about three minutes each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. One coin among many is heavier, and you have five weighings.
screens.question: What is the largest number of coins you can always handle?

hints.text: Each weighing has three outcomes.
Five weighings give $3^5$ outcomes.
$3^5 = 243$, and thirds reach it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the outcomes of five weighings.

byKey.thirtytwo: That is $2^5$, for tests with two outcomes. A balance has three.
byKey.fifteen: You multiplied 3 by 5. Outcomes multiply, so raise 3 to the fifth power.
byKey.onetwentyone: That is $(3^5 - 1)/2$, for a fake that may be heavy or light.

explain.text: Five weighings give $3^5 = 243$ outcomes, so at most 243 coins. Thirds reach it: 243, 81, 27, 9, 3, 1. Principle: $k$ weighings handle $3^k$ coins with one heavy fake.

screens.title: Drill: fifty coins
screens.prose: Drill, about three minutes. Fifty coins, one heavier.
screens.question: What is the fewest weighings that always finds it?

hints.text: Find the smallest power of 3 at least 50.
Four weighings. Split 50 as 17, 17 and 16.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare 50 with the powers of 3.

byKey.three: Three weighings handle 27 coins at most.
byKey.five: Five weighings work, but four already do: $3^4 = 81 \ge 50$.

explain.text: Three weighings handle 27 coins, too few; four handle 81. Split 50 as 17, 17 and 16, then 6, 6, 5, then 2, 2, 2, then 1, 1, 0. Principle: the smallest $k$ with $3^k \ge n$.

screens.title: Drill: one bag of fakes
screens.prose: Drill, about three minutes. Eight bags of coins. Genuine coins weigh 5 g; one bag holds only fakes of 6 g. You take $k$ coins from bag $k$ and weigh them all once on a digital scale. It reads 185 g.
screens.question: Which bag holds the fakes?

hints.text: How much would the 36 coins weigh if all were genuine?
Each fake adds 1 g, and bag $k$ gave $k$ coins.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the reading with the all-genuine weight.

byKey.thirtysix: 36 is the number of coins taken. The extra weight names the bag.
byKey.eight: That is the number of bags. Use the extra 5 g.

explain.text: Taking $1 + 2 + \dots + 8 = 36$ coins gives 180 g if all are genuine. The extra 5 g means five fakes, so bag 5. Principle: give each suspect its own signature, so one reading names it.

screens.title: Four weighings, heavy or light
screens.prose: Follow-up. The interviewer allows four weighings, and you must also say heavy or light, with no coin known to be genuine. Bisecting a failing commit is the same count: $k$ pass or fail tests separate $2^k$ commits.
screens.question: What is the largest number of coins you can always handle?

hints.text: Twelve coins was the answer for three weighings. What formula gives 12?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each coin is 2 cases, and you lose a little to the first weighing.

byKey.forty: Forty coins give 80 cases, under 81, but no first weighing works without a genuine coin. With one extra genuine coin, 40 do work.
byKey.eightyone: Each coin is two cases, heavy or light, so 81 outcomes cover far fewer coins.
byKey.twelve: Twelve is the answer for three weighings.

explain.text: With no coin known to be genuine, $k$ weighings handle $(3^k - 3)/2$ coins: 12 for three, 39 for four. A search of every plan confirms 39 and rules out 40. Principle: count cases against outcomes, then check the first weighing.

ideas: A balance has three outcomes, so $k$ weighings tell apart at most $3^k$ cases.
Split the suspects into three groups as equal as possible; every outcome keeps at most a third.
A fake that may be heavy or light doubles the cases: 12 coins in 3 weighings, 39 in 4.

formula.name: Weighing bound
formula.note: Heavy only: $n \le 3^k$. Heavy or light, no genuine coin: $n \le (3^k - 3)/2$.

summary.trap: Halving wastes the level outcome: nine coins take 2 weighings, not 3.

quiz.prose: Thirteen coins, one fake heavier or lighter, three weighings. Now you also hold one extra coin known to be genuine.
quiz.question: Can you always find the fake and say heavy or light?

options.why: The extra coin changes the first weighing: 5 against 4 plus the genuine coin fits both bounds.
26 is less than 27. The count allows it, and the genuine coin removes the obstacle.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The genuine coin lets the pans hold different numbers of suspects.

byKey.no: Without help 13 fail, but the genuine coin lets you weigh 5 suspects against 4 plus it.
byKey.count: 26 is fewer than 27, so the count allows it.

explain.text: With a genuine coin, weigh 5 suspects against 4 suspects and the genuine coin. A tilt leaves 9 cases and level leaves 4 coins, 8 cases, both within 9. A search confirms 13 can be done, and 14 cannot.

quiz.question: What is the fewest weighings that always finds it?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare 10 with the powers of 3.

byKey.two: Two weighings handle 9 coins at most.

explain.text: Two weighings give 9 outcomes, one short of 10 coins. Three give 27: weigh 3 against 3 with 4 aside, and so on. Principle: the smallest $k$ with $3^k \ge n$.

quiz.prose: Twenty-seven coins, one heavier, three weighings.
quiz.question: Which first weighing keeps the plan within three?

options.why: If it tips, 13 suspects remain for two weighings, which handle 9.
If it tips, 10 suspects remain for two weighings, one too many.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Every outcome must leave at most 9.

byKey.thirteen: A tilt leaves 13 suspects, more than two weighings can handle.
byKey.ten: A tilt leaves 10 suspects, more than 9.

explain.text: Two weighings handle 9 suspects, so each outcome must leave 9 or fewer. Only 9, 9 and 9 does that for 27. Principle: split into equal thirds.
